messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nikolai was a 26-year-old European American fisherman who came to treatment after months of feeling as if his life had narrowed around one night he could not get out of his head. During a trip at sea, he had been seized, beaten, and tortured by men who wanted information he did not have. He described being forced into a position that left his body twisted and pinned, with blows landing repeatedly in the same places, until pain became the only thing he could think about. Now, when the memory returned, it did not come to him as a distant story but as a bodily replay: his shoulders tightened, his chest and ribs seemed to ache in the same spots, and he felt himself back in that same contorted position. Along with the physical sensation came a rush of rage so intense that he could hardly bear to sit still when he thought about what had been done to him.

At first, the reminders seemed to find him in ordinary places. A baby crying in a shop or at a neighbor’s apartment could suddenly pull him back into the worst moments, not because the sound itself was dangerous, but because it brought the memory rushing up with such force that he felt trapped inside it again. Riding the bus to the docks could do the same: the confined space, the proximity to strangers, and the inability to control who was around him made him feel emotionally exposed in a way that opened the door to those same images and sensations. When that happened, the memory was not just something he recalled; it filled his body with the old pain and rage, and he became afraid of what his own reactions might be. He said that after a trigger hit, he would spend the rest of the day on edge, convinced that if he let himself feel too much he would break apart or lose control.

That fear had started to shape the way he moved through the world. Nikolai preferred to sit with his back against a wall so he could see the whole room, and if a chair was not positioned that way he would keep adjusting it until it was. He listened constantly for sounds that might mean someone was coming into the house, especially at night, and he scanned every environment for potential weapons or dangerous objects without meaning to. He had come to believe that if he could stay alert enough, he might catch danger before it reached him; at the same time, the more he watched for threat, the more exposed he felt, and the more likely it seemed that a reminder would break through. In that state of guardfulness, ordinary cues became potent again. A baby’s cry on the bus, a doorway he could not monitor, even the feeling of being emotionally vulnerable with his wife after a difficult day could set off the same alarm, because once he felt unsafe he seemed to notice every sound, every object, every possible angle of attack. Those sharpened senses brought the torture back into view, and the memory in turn made the world feel even more dangerous.

Over the following months, he began organizing his days around avoiding those moments. He took longer routes to skip buses when he could, turned down invitations to crowded family gatherings, and grew quieter at home because being emotionally open felt like a risk he could not afford. The changes strained his marriage; his wife noticed how often he checked the locks and how little he could relax when they were together. At work on the fishing boat and at the dock, he functioned, but he did so with one part of him always listening and scanning, as if any environment might hold the same threat as that night at sea. By the time he sought help, Nikolai was exhausted by how quickly a cry, a ride across town, or a moment of openness could bring back the pain, the rage, and the sense of being pinned in place. What frightened him most was that he no longer trusted himself to stay present when the memories hit, and what he hoped for was some way to stop living as though danger were always just behind the next sound or in the next room.
